instruction: Can I sleep with the lights on? I don't like the dark in here.
response: Of course — you can absolutely have a light on. There's usually a small night light in the room that's much softer than the overhead lights, and your nurse can help you find the setting that feels right. Some kids like a little bit of light, some like the overhead off but a lamp on, and some want it fully dark. Your comfort matters and there's no rule that says it has to be dark. Just tell your nurse what you need and they'll set it up for you.

instruction: What happens if I accidentally press the button on my bed?
response: Don't worry — there's no penalty for accidentally pressing a button. If a nurse comes in because you pressed the call button by mistake, just tell them it was an accident and they'll simply check that you're okay and head back. That button is there to help you and nurses would much rather have a false alarm than have you need something and not press it. If you're worried about pressing something you shouldn't, ask your nurse to point out which buttons do what — most of the controls are really simple once someone explains them.

instruction: My mom brought my favourite snacks from home. Am I allowed to eat them?
response: It depends on what your care team has said about your diet. Some kids are on specific diets because of their condition or because they have a test or procedure coming up — in those cases, certain foods need to be approved first. Check with your nurse before eating anything from home, just to be safe. In many cases it's completely fine, and having a taste of something familiar from home can actually really help with how you're feeling. Your nurse just needs to give the go-ahead so it doesn't interfere with your treatment.

instruction: Can I wear my own pyjamas instead of the hospital ones?
response: Yes, in most cases you can wear your own pyjamas or comfortable clothes — most kids actually prefer it. Your care team just needs easy access to wherever an IV or monitor might be attached, so loose-fitting clothes work best. If you're having a procedure that requires a hospital gown, your nurse will let you know ahead of time. Otherwise, bring whatever comfortable clothes from home make you feel most like yourself.

instruction: How come they woke me up at night to check on me? I was sleeping.
response: It's one of the frustrating parts of being in hospital — your nurses need to check on you at regular intervals even during the night because some important things, like your blood pressure or how a medicine is working, need to be monitored on a schedule that doesn't stop for sleep. It's not to bother you — it's because they're taking good care of you. If the overnight checks are making it really hard to sleep, you can talk to your nurse about whether any of them could be adjusted, done more gently, or combined so there are fewer interruptions. Sometimes small changes are possible.

instruction: Is my little sister allowed to come visit even though she's only four?
response: Children can usually visit, but there are specific rules about visitors at Children's Hospital that depend on the unit and the current health situation on the ward. Very young children sometimes have age restrictions on certain floors during things like cold and flu season, to protect patients who might be more vulnerable. Your nurse is the best person to check with — just ask 'My four-year-old sister wants to visit; is that okay on this unit right now?' They'll tell you exactly what the current rules are and what your sister would need to do, like washing her hands and making sure she's not recently been sick.

instruction: Do I have to stay in my room the whole time or can I walk around?
response: Whether you can walk around depends on how you're feeling and what your care team has said. Some kids need to stay in bed or in their room because of their treatment, and some are able to move around the unit. If you're not sure, ask your nurse: 'Am I allowed to walk around?' If you can, there may be a playroom, a common area, or hallways you're welcome to explore. Getting up and moving when it's medically okay is actually a good thing for your body and your mood. Your nurse will let you know what's safe for you specifically.

instruction: What time do the lights have to go off at night?
response: There's no strict 'lights out' rule that applies to every room — it's more about being considerate of others if you're sharing a room. In your own space, you can keep your light on as long as you need to. The hospital does try to keep hallways quieter and dimmer overnight so everyone can rest, but your personal light is your call. If you want to read or use your tablet at night, that's generally fine. Just keep the sound low if you're sharing a room so your neighbour can sleep too.

instruction: Can my dad sleep here with me tonight?
response: Yes — at Children's Hospital, parents and guardians are welcome to stay overnight with their child. There's usually a recliner or pull-out cot in the room for them. If your dad wants to stay, just let your nurse know and they'll make sure he has somewhere comfortable to rest. Having a parent stay the night is really common and the staff are used to it — it can make a big difference in how safe and settled you feel. If there's any reason a specific night might be harder (like a very early procedure), your nurse can help plan around it.

instruction: My tablet died and I didn't bring my charger. What do I do?
response: First, ask your nurse — they often have a collection of common chargers that previous families have left behind, or know where to find one. You can also ask a family member to bring your charger from home. Some units have a charging station or can point you to a nearby one. In the meantime, the hospital has wifi, so if someone can bring a device or charger, you'll be back online quickly. Don't underestimate how much having your own entertainment matters — the staff want you to have it and will usually try to help.

instruction: My phone is my main way of managing my anxiety. Is there any rule about using it at night?
response: There's no hospital-wide rule against using your phone at night. The general consideration is keeping noise low if you're in a shared room. If using your phone — whether for music, meditation apps, messaging, or just something to focus on — helps you manage anxiety, that's a legitimate reason and worth mentioning to your care team. They may have additional suggestions, but they're not going to take your coping tool away. If the anxiety itself is significantly affecting your sleep or wellbeing, that's also worth raising as something to address directly — there are supports available specifically for that.

instruction: My medication schedule at home is different from what they're giving me here. Should I say something?
response: Yes, definitely say something — this is important. When you're admitted, your care team reviews your home medications and may adjust timing, dose, or delivery method for clinical reasons. But they can also make mistakes or miss something. If you're noticing a difference that doesn't have an explanation you've been given, bring it up with your nurse or physician directly: 'At home I take X at Y time — can you tell me why it's different here?' Medication reconciliation is a standard part of hospital care, and your input as the person who knows your own regimen is valuable.

instruction: I need to exercise every day or I can't sleep. That's not possible here.
response: It might be more possible than you think, depending on your mobility and what your care team allows. Ask your nurse or doctor what physical activity is appropriate for your current situation. For many patients, walking the hallway, gentle stretching, or bodyweight movements in the room are permitted and even encouraged. A physiotherapist can also be consulted to suggest safe activity options given your specific condition. It's worth being direct: 'Exercise is important to my mental health and sleep — what can I do while I'm here?' That framing usually gets a more helpful response than asking if you're 'allowed' to move.

instruction: I want to shower in the morning but the nurse comes around really early. Can I tell them not to come in during that time?
response: Yes — establishing a routine that works for you is a reasonable ask. Let your nurse know at the start of their shift or the night before: 'I like to shower in the morning around X time — can you plan around that if possible?' Many aspects of morning rounds can be slightly flexible. The ones that can't be moved are usually time-sensitive medications or monitoring, and your nurse can tell you which those are. For everything else, there's often more flexibility than it might seem. Communicating your preferences doesn't make you difficult; it helps the team schedule around you.

instruction: I need to take my own medication at a specific time every day. How does that work here?
response: When you're admitted, you should disclose all medications you take at home — including the timing and dosage. Your care team will review them and either continue them, adjust them, or provide hospital equivalents. If a specific timing is medically important (like a medication that needs to be taken with food at a consistent time, or a hormonal medication), note that explicitly so it's flagged. Once you're admitted, medications at Children's Hospital are administered by nurses on schedule, but that schedule is built around your needs. Ask your nurse: 'My home medication needs to be given at X time for [reason] — how do we handle that here?'

instruction: Is there a curfew for when visitors have to leave?
response: Yes, visiting hours are structured at Children's Hospital, though parents and legal guardians generally have more flexibility than other visitors. The specific times vary by unit, and the current rules can change based on what's happening on the ward. Ask your nurse what the visiting hours are for your specific unit and what exceptions exist. If a particular visit matters to you — a friend who can only come at an unusual time, for example — it's worth asking whether an exception is possible rather than assuming it isn't. Many units are reasonably accommodating when there's a clear reason.

instruction: Can I order food from outside if the hospital menu doesn't work for me?
response: Depending on your diet restrictions and your care team's guidance, outside food is sometimes possible. If you're on a medically prescribed diet, anything from outside needs to be compatible with it — check with your nurse or dietitian first. If there are no dietary restrictions and the hospital menu just doesn't appeal to you, families often bring food in. Delivery to the hospital is technically possible but can be complicated — having family pick it up and bring it is more reliable. Let your nurse know what you need and they can tell you exactly what's allowed in your situation.

instruction: I'm in a shared room and my roommate is making it really hard to rest.
response: That's a legitimate concern — rest is genuinely part of your recovery. Start by telling your nurse specifically what the issue is: noise, lighting, visitor times, something else. Nurses can often mediate or adjust visiting schedules to make shared rooms more manageable. If the situation is significantly affecting your ability to recover, ask directly whether a private room is available. Private rooms are sometimes allocated based on clinical need, so framing it as an impact on your health and sleep gives your team something to work with. You're not being unreasonable for needing conditions where you can actually rest.

instruction: I need to pray at specific times every day. How does that work here?
response: Religious and spiritual practices are respected at Children's Hospital. There's a chapel and spiritual care team available to all patients. For prayer at specific times, let your nurse know your schedule — they can plan around it where possible so you're not interrupted or called for something during those times. If you need a quiet private space, your nurse can help find one or arrange for privacy in your room. There's also a chaplain available who works with patients of all faiths and no faith — they can help connect you with specific supports if needed.

instruction: I don't want anyone to visit me. How do I make that actually happen?
response: You can make this official. Talk to your nurse and ask to have a 'no visitors' note placed on your room — this gives staff something to point to rather than putting you in the position of turning people away yourself. You can make exceptions for specific people (like one parent) while excluding others. Your privacy is taken seriously and you don't have to justify why you don't want visitors. If specific people are persisting despite being told, that escalates to a more formal conversation with the unit, but a simple documented preference is usually enough to handle it.
